title: Episode 325: George III (Part 2): The Madness of King George, Trafalgar, Waterloo, and the Regency
description:
The heartbreaking, epic second half of King George III's historic reign. In 1788, the King was struck by a terrifying, mysterious mental breakdown—now believed to be acute porphyria or bipolar mania—in which he talked for hours until foaming at the mouth. Subjected to horrific eighteenth-century medical treatments by Dr. Willis, George's recovery was celebrated with nationwide ecstasy. Guiding Britain through the titanic global struggle against the French Revolution and Napoleon Bonaparte, George inspired his people through Nelson's triumph at Trafalgar and Wellington's victory at Waterloo. Sinking into permanent blindness, deafness, and dementia at Windsor during the Prince Regent's era, discover the tragic passing of Farmer George.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series concludes our two-part saga of King George III: exploring the terrifying medical mystery of the King's madness, the titanic struggle against Napoleon, and the poignant, forgotten twilight of a legendary monarch. Here is George with part two of George the Third.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE FIRST MADNESS: THE AUTUMN OF 1788
In October 1788, at Windsor Castle, fifty-year-old King George III was struck down by a sudden, terrifying medical catastrophe. The King developed severe stomach cramps, joint pain, dark reddish urine, and fell into a state of hyperactive manic delirium. He spoke non-stop for nineteen consecutive hours until his voice was cracked and he foamed at the mouth, suffered violent convulsions, and failed to recognize his beloved Queen Charlotte. Legend claimed he shook hands with an oak tree in Windsor Great Park believing it was the King of Prussia. Modern medical historians debate whether George suffered from acute intermittent porphyria—a genetic metabolic disorder affecting the nervous system—or severe bipolar mania complicated by toxic arsenic contained in court medicines. The King's physicians were utterly baffled, subjecting the sovereign to barbaric treatments: bleeding him with leeches, applying blistering plasters of Spanish fly to his legs, and restraining the monarch in an iron-and-leather 'restraining chair' whenever he became agitated, reducing the King of Great Britain to a weeping, humiliated captive. The King's sudden descent into madness in the autumn of 1788 was an agonizing medical horror: his pulse raced at one hundred and forty beats a minute, his skin was burning with fever, and his speech was an unstoppable torrent of manic delirium, reciting poetry, barking like a dog, and speaking with long-dead ancestors. Dr. Francis Willis, an unorthodox physician and clergyman who ran a private asylum in Lincolnshire, insisted on treating the monarch like an ordinary patient: he forced the King into a straitjacket whenever he was violent and applied blisters to his head. Yet Willis also understood the importance of fresh air, conversation, and physical exercise, managing the King with firm kindness until the fever miraculously broke in February 1789.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE REGENCY CRISIS AND THE TRIUMPHANT RECOVERY: 1789
The King's madness precipitated a vicious constitutional crisis in Parliament: the 'Regency Crisis'. The Prince of Wales, a debauched, spendthrift Whig who despised his father, allied with Charles James Fox to demand immediate, unlimited regency powers so they could seize government patronage and dismiss William Pitt. Pitt fought a brilliant delaying action in the House of Commons, introducing a Regency Bill with strict limitations. In February 1789, under the firm, humane psychological management of Dr. Francis Willis, an astonishing miracle occurred: King George's fever broke, his mental faculties cleared, and he regained complete sanity. When the King emerged from Windsor, nationwide celebrations erupted: church bells pealed, bonfires blazed, and in April 1789, the King and Queen attended a colossal Thanksgiving service at St. Paul's Cathedral before sixty thousand weeping citizens. The King's popularity soared to unprecedented heights, cementing an unshakeable bond of affection between George and the British people. The thanksgiving celebrations at St. Paul's Cathedral in April 1789 were a staggering demonstration of popular devotion to the recovered monarch. Sixty thousand cheering citizens lined the route from Whitehall to St. Paul's, waving handkerchiefs and throwing flowers before the royal carriage. Inside the great dome, as five thousand charity school children sang the Hundredth Psalm, King George broke down in humble tears of gratitude. The recovery thwarted the greedy ambitions of the Prince of Wales and Charles James Fox, keeping William Pitt firmly in power on the very eve of the French Revolution.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE FRENCH REVOLUTION AND THE DEFENSE OF BRITAIN: 1793 TO 1800
Barely had the King recovered when the French Revolution erupted across the Channel, executing King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette in 1793. When revolutionary France declared war on Britain, King George became the stalwart symbol of British constitutional order, Protestant stability, and national defiance against Jacobin terror. George survived multiple assassination attempts by revolutionary sympathizers: in 1795, a stone shattered his state coach window on his way to Parliament, and in May 1800, at Drury Lane Theatre, a deranged former soldier fired two pistol shots at the royal box. George stepped calmly forward to the edge of the box, bowed to the terrified audience, and commanded the performance to proceed, winning thunderous cheers. In 1800, following the Irish Rebellion of 1798, George signed the historic Act of Union, uniting Great Britain and Ireland into the United Kingdom on January 1, 1801, formally dropping the archaic title 'King of France' from the royal style after four hundred and sixty years. During the terrifying years of the French Revolution, King George was the steadfast anchor of the British nation. When the deranged former soldier James Hadfield fired two pistol shots at the King in the royal box at Drury Lane Theatre in May 1800, the musket balls burying themselves in the ceiling twelve inches above George's head, the King showed magnificent composure: he ordered the performance of She Would and She Would Not to proceed, taking a nap during the second act. The audience erupted in hysterical cheers, singing 'God Save the King' three times, viewing their brave, moral sovereign as the living fortress of British constitutional liberty against foreign anarchy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: TRAFALGAR AND THE DEATH OF PITT: 1805 TO 1806
The rise of Napoleon Bonaparte brought Britain into an existential struggle for national survival. In 1804, Napoleon massed an invasion army of one hundred and fifty thousand men at Boulogne, awaiting a French naval fleet to control the English Channel for six hours. On October 21, 1805, off Cape Trafalgar, Admiral Lord Nelson deployed his daring tactical battle plan, sailing two columns directly into the Franco-Spanish line. In five hours of carnage, Nelson destroyed twenty-two enemy warships without losing a single British vessel, ending Napoleon's dreams of invading Britain forever. When news reached Windsor that Nelson had fallen in the moment of victory, King George wept, declaring that Nelson's loss had eclipsed the glory of the victory. Three months later, in January 1806, forty-six-year-old Prime Minister William Pitt died of exhaustion and gout, his final whispered words: 'Oh, my country! How I love my country!' King George mourned the loss of the brilliant minister who had been the pillar of his throne for over twenty years. The Battle of Trafalgar in October 1805 was the naval masterpiece that saved Britain from invasion. Nelson's famous signal flying from HMS Victory—'England expects that every man will do his duty'—became the immortal creed of the Royal Navy. When the shattered French and Spanish fleet surrendered and news reached London of Nelson's death, the nation was plunged into simultaneous ecstasy and profound grief. King George was so moved by Nelson's sacrifice that he ordered a monumental state funeral in St. Paul's Cathedral, the first non-royal state funeral in modern British history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE PRINCESS AMELIA AND THE FINAL DESCENT: 1810
In 1810, King George celebrated his Golden Jubilee—fifty years upon the British throne—amid grand pageantry and public celebrations. But personal tragedy was about to extinguish the King's mind forever. George's beloved youngest child, Princess Amelia, contracted fatal tuberculosis. The King visited his twenty-seven-year-old daughter daily, weeping by her bedside. In October 1810, Amelia slipped a ring containing a lock of her hair and the inscription 'Remember Me' onto her father's finger. Days later, Amelia died. The grief broke seventy-two-year-old King George completely: his madness returned with terrifying, irreversible permanence. In February 1811, Parliament passed the Regency Act, appointing the Prince of Wales as Prince Regent. King George III vanished behind the thick stone walls of Windsor Castle, never to appear in public again. The death of Princess Amelia in November 1810 was the final, fatal blow to King George's fragile mind. Amelia had been her father's darling child, riding beside him at Weymouth and playing the piano for him as his eyesight failed. When she placed the lock of hair upon his finger on her deathbed, whispering 'Remember Me', George wept uncontrollably. Within days of her funeral, the King's manic delirium returned with permanent ferocity: he spent his nights pacing his rooms at Windsor, shouting that Amelia was not dead but living in Hanover, singing hymns and refusing to eat, sinking into the dark, silent oblivion of the Regency.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE GHOST IN THE NORTH TERRACE: THE REGENCY YEARS: 1811 TO 1819
For the final decade of his life, George lived as an ethereal ghost in a suite of padded rooms overlooking the North Terrace of Windsor Castle. He was completely blind from cataracts and stone-deaf from ear infections. Dressed in a long violet dressing gown, with a magnificent flowing white beard reaching to his waist and wild silver hair, the King lived in a parallel reality of his own imagination. He held conversations with long-dead ministers and angels, played hymns on his harpsichord from memory, and conducted imaginary parliaments. He believed that he had died and was residing in heaven. Yet outside his silent prison, his kingdom triumphed: in June 1815, the Duke of Wellington defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo, securing British supremacy across the globe. King George never knew that Napoleon had been banished to St. Helena or that his empire was victorious. In November 1818, Queen Charlotte died, but court physicians did not dare inform the blind, deaf king that his wife of fifty-seven years was gone. The decade of the Regency from 1811 to 1820 was a magnificent cultural era of dandyism, Beau Brummell, Jane Austen, Lord Byron, and John Nash's London architecture, presided over by the extravagant, spendthrift Prince Regent. Yet in the isolated private apartments of Windsor Castle, the blind, deaf old King lived in complete seclusion. He wore a plain dressing gown, never combed his long white beard, and spent his days playing Handel's Messiah on his harpsichord. He was entirely unaware that the Duke of Wellington had defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815, or that his kingdom was now the supreme master of the globe.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PASSING OF THE PATRIARCH: WINDSOR: JANUARY 29, 1820
In January 1820, eighty-one-year-old King George III's physical strength finally ebbed away. Unable to eat or walk, he lay quietly in his bed at Windsor Castle surrounded by his doctors. On the evening of Saturday, January 29, 1820, at eight thirty-eight in the evening, King George III died peacefully, holding the hand of his second son, the Duke of York. He had reigned for fifty-nine years, three months, and four days—the longest reign of any male monarch in British history. His colossal state funeral at St. George's Chapel in Windsor was illuminated by thousands of flickering torchlights. Though history remembered him for the loss of the American colonies, the British people mourned him as an affectionate patriarch of unmatched moral integrity, decency, and fortitude, who had steered Great Britain through the greatest existential storm in modern history into an era of global supremacy. When King George III died peacefully at Windsor on January 29, 1820, at the age of eighty-one, the entire British Empire fell into deep, respectful silence. He had reigned for nearly sixty years, witnessing the loss of America, the Industrial Revolution, the defeat of Napoleon, and the rise of the British Empire. Though his early political obstinacy had alienated the American colonies, his personal integrity, devotion to family, and steadfast courage during the Napoleonic crisis had transformed the British monarchy into an enduring, beloved national institution, remembered by his subjects not as a tyrant, but as honest, noble Farmer George.

[Rebecca - Host]
